catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress occurs mostly on the penultimate syllable in morphologically simple words. Morphologically complex words with more than 3 syllables vary with the stress on the antepenultimate syllable or on a syllable further to the front in the word. Morphologically complex words, especially verbs, can become quite long, up to 7 or 8 syllables. So far no regular rule has been found as far as the stress placement goes. 'bule 'big' do'fene 'pig' ua 'all' kele'bulu 'animal' kele'bulumo 'animal (in focus)' hili'sesu '1st person think' di'digifasia 'having carried one by one' hilise'mabiyo 'don't think (worry)' siba'gafasia 'having emptied the mumu' hili'sesenaga 'if you think'

new_statements.rule_in_words: In morphologically simple words stress is (mostly) on the penultimate syllable ('bule, do'fene, kele'bulu). In morphologically complex words of more than three syllables, especially long verbs (up to 7-8 syllables), stress is on the antepenult or a syllable further to the left (kele'bulumo, hilise'mabiyo, hili'sesenaga, di'digifasia, siba'gafasia), and the authors found no regular rule for its placement. The examples are consistent with stress staying near the stem rather than counting from the word edge, but the source does not claim that.
new_statements.exceptions: 'mostly' penultimate even in simple words (no exceptions listed); morphologically complex words >3 syllables are described as variable with no regular rule found; hili'sesu (penult) vs hilise'mabiyo and hili'sesenaga (antepenult) from the same verb stem.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; citation forms from an SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet (draft, no peer review). Language listed as 'Onobasulu Language [ONN], Southern Highlands Province'; no dialect specified. Nasalisation and (marginal) vowel length are the other suprasegmentals; no tone.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD names the language 'Onobasulu Language [ONN]', Southern Highlands Province (Walagu village area), population c. 800, with no dialect stated; Shaw 1986 spells it 'Onabasulu'. Same languoid as onob1238.
